summary.text: Nuclear fission is a reaction in which the nucleus of an atom splits into two or more smaller nuclei.
It often produces neutrons and gamma rays, and splitting one uranium-235 atom releases about 100 million times the energy of burning one carbon atom in air.
Since a splitting nucleus emits more neutrons than it absorbs, a chain reaction is possible, and nuclear power plants and weapons both rely on it.

facts.label: Who named it
facts.value: Frisch, by analogy with the fission of living cells

facts.label: First proof
facts.value: Hahn and Strassmann proved it on 19 December 1938

facts.label: Chain-reaction isotopes
facts.value: U-233, U-235 and Pu-239 can sustain a chain reaction

facts.label: Three-piece splits
facts.value: Ternary fission happens 2 to 4 times per 1000 events

facts.label: Spontaneous fission
facts.value: Discovered in 1940, it needs no neutron to start

items.prompt: A uranium nucleus absorbs one neutron and splits. What allows the reaction to keep itself going?

options.label: The nucleus soaks up neutrons from the fuel rods around it
The nucleus gives off more neutrons than the one it absorbed
The gamma rays it emits turn into new neutrons right away
The split fragments pull in fresh neutrons from the air

items.explain: A fissioning nucleus emits more neutrons than the one it absorbs, which makes a chain reaction possible.

items.prompt: A physicist repeats an alpha decay many times, then a fission many times. What does she find about the products?

options.label: Both give identical products every time
Alpha decay gives varied products, while fission gives identical ones
Both give products that vary in a chaotic way
Fission products vary widely, while alpha decay gives the same ones each time

items.explain: The unpredictable composition of fission products distinguishes it from purely quantum tunneling processes such as alpha decay, which give the same products each time.

items.prompt: For a splitting nucleus to give out energy overall, what must hold for its fragments compared with the parent?

options.label: Their total binding energy must be greater than the parent's
Their total binding energy must be less than the parent's
They must have exactly the same size as each other
They must outnumber the protons in the parent nucleus

items.explain: For fission to produce energy, the total binding energy of the resulting elements must be greater than that of the starting element.

items.prompt: A heavy atom splits into fragments. Why do physicists call this a nuclear transmutation?

options.label: The fragments fuse back together into the original atom
The splitting happens only when the atom is heated
The fragments are not the same element as the parent atom
The atom gives off a great deal of energy while splitting

items.explain: Fission is a form of nuclear transmutation because the resulting fragments are not the same element as the original parent atom.

items.prompt: A reactor slows fast neutrons down so they can split its fuel easily. What kind of nuclide is that fuel?

options.label: Fissile, easily split by slow neutrons
Fissionable, mostly split by fast neutrons
Stable, one that never splits at all
Spontaneous, one that needs no neutron

items.explain: Fissile nuclides easily split with slow, thermal neutrons, which usually come from moderating fast neutrons, while fissionable nuclides primarily split with fast neutrons.

items.prompt: Some very heavy nuclei split with no neutron hitting them at all. What makes that possible?

options.label: A passing gamma ray gives them a nudge
The nucleus is already unstable from having too many neutrons
They cool down and the pieces separate
A chain reaction starts from a nearby nucleus

items.explain: In spontaneous fission, the nucleus is already unstable from an overabundance of neutrons, and it occurs in very high-mass-number isotopes.
